proposed_features.description: The geometric outline of the tail feathers when extended or at rest is a primary structural differentiator between the larger, wedge-shaped species and the smaller, rounded species.
The relative robustness and depth of the beak distinguishes the heavy-billed species from the slender-billed species.
The degree of downward curve on the upper mandible varies significantly, with some species having a distinct hook and others having a straighter profile.
The overall scale of the bird relative to its environment or standard proportions separates the large corvids from the smaller passerines.
The presence of metallic sheens (purple, blue, green) in the feathers is a key visual marker for specific species, particularly in certain lighting conditions.
The texture of the feathers on the throat and upper breast, ranging from smooth and sleek to shaggy and spiky, is a distinct morphological trait.
The color of the iris, which can range from dark brown to a distinct pale blue or grey, helps differentiate the species.
The length of the legs relative to the body size and the height of the stance provides a proportional cue for identification.
The profile of the head, including the slope of the forehead and the overall roundness, varies between the species.
The shape of the primary feathers at the wingtips, which can be pointed or rounded, is visible in flight or perched poses.
The typical resting or foraging posture, such as a hunched back or an upright stance, is characteristic of specific species.
The width of the beak at the base where it meets the face, which can be broad and heavy or narrow and delicate.
The length of the tail relative to the body length, which is longer in some species and shorter in others.
The consistency of the black coloration across the body, with some species showing distinct color variations or sheens while others are uniformly dark.
